papers.title: Reframing marine host-microbe symbioses: from taxonomic inventories to functional convergence
papers.abstract: In October 2025, the Trends in Host-Microbe Symbioses Symposium at the University of Padova (Italy) brought together a global community of researchers, with the aim of taking stock of the current trajectory of marine host-microbiome research. Integrating perspectives from ecology, evolution, biogeochemistry, and biotechnology, the symposium documented a clear transition from descriptive surveys of microbial diversity toward a mechanistic understanding of host–microbe interactions. Across an unusually broad taxonomic spectrum – corals, sponges, fishes, molluscs, algae and seagrasses, cnidarians, acoels, arthropods and mammals - microbiomes were consistently framed as integral components of host biology, shaping nutrient cycling, development, immunity, and ecosystem function. Despite phylogenetic diversity across host groups, convergent functional processes (notably N and C cycling, stress buffering, immune priming, and metabolic complementation) emerged as a unifying framework, even though their taxonomic underpinnings remained system-specific. Advances in multi-omics, spatially resolved imaging (MALDI-MSI, NanoSIMS, FISH/CARD-FISH) and experimental microbiome manipulation are increasingly linking microbial identity to activity and function, enabling early predictive frameworks across scales. Collectively, the symposium laid the groundwork for microbiome-based interventions to enhance host resilience and support ecosystem conservation in a rapidly changing ocean.

papers.title: Distinct seasonal acclimatisation trajectories characterize transplanted and natural meadow seagrass plants
papers.abstract: Abstract Successful establishment is a critical determinant of seagrass restoration, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying seedling acclimatisation to natural environments remain poorly understood. Here, we combined seasonal physiological observations, transcriptome profiling, and gene co-expression network analysis to investigate the mechanisms underlying the early post-transplantation phase of Posidonia oceanica , a dominant foundation seagrass species, following transplantation. Transplanted seedlings were compared with plants from adjacent natural meadows over the first six months after transplantation using leaf and root samples collected in spring, summer, and autumn. Tissue identity was the primary driver of transcriptomic variation, but transplanted seedlings remained transcriptionally distinct from plants in natural meadows throughout the study, with roots showing greater divergence than leaves, suggesting tissue-specific trajectories of post-transplantation acclimatisation. The early post-transplantation phase was characterised by the activation of genes associated with RNA processing, transcriptional regulation, and abscisic acid signalling. During a summer marine heatwave (28 °C), both plant groups induced conserved heat-response pathways, including heat-shock proteins and protein-folding mechanisms. Furthermore, transplanted seedlings maintained higher expression of genes involved in photosystem II repair and photoprotection and exhibited reduced leaf growth and extensive leaf necrosis, consistent with a greater requirement for photosynthetic maintenace under prolonged thermal stress. Gene co-expression network analysis revealed that regulatory networks governing structural integrity, hormone signalling, and defence were more stable in natural meadow plants, while transplanted seedlings progressively reorganized their gene co-expression patterns to resemble those of natural meadow plants, particularly in leaves. Our findings reveal tissue-specific molecular trajectories of acclimatisation during early seedling establishment and identify candidate molecular indicators of field acclimatisation and thermal stress responses, providing new mechanistic insights relevant to seedling-based seagrass restoration under climate change.

papers.title: An Isolated Hyposaline River Occurrence of Birsteiniolla (Foraminifera) From Western Australia, Previously Known From Central Asian Lakes and Interior Seas
papers.abstract: A low diversity foraminiferal assemblage inhabits a hyposaline stretch of the Jerdacuttup River, which flows into Jerdacuttup Lakes near Hopetoun, south coast Western Australia, but is not connected, at least by any surface flows, to the open Southern Ocean. Among the six species of foraminifera identified is an organic-cemented agglutinated type ( Birsteiniolla gr. macrostoma ) that is morphologically like Birsteiniolla macrostoma Yankovskaya and Mikhalevich known only from Central Asian lakes and interior seas (e.g., Lake Issyk-Kul’, Caspian and Aral seas). In late 2016 sampling it was very abundant on stems of Ruppia seagrass that form meadows on the river floor but was very rare in September 2019 when the organic-cemented agglutinated Scherochorella gr. barwonensis was abundant on the seagrass. Foraminiferal distributions are patchy in the river’s muddy sediment. The calcitic rotaliine Ammonia haigi is the most abundant species and is morphologically close to Ammonia caspica from Central Asia, as is the other common calcitic rotaliine species identified here, Cribroelphidium sp. cf. C. revetsi , which is close to Cribroelphidium caspicum from Central Asia. The other foraminiferal species are Miliammina ? sp. and Trochammina gr. inflata , both with similar morphotypes recognized globally. It is speculated that the Jerdacuttup River foraminifera were transported via water birds (probably in their digestive tracts) on the East Asian–Australasian Avian Flyway. The migration pathway may have involved local migration between the isolated Australian river systems as well as the intercontinental migration, leading to some potential genetic diversification. A three-point research strategy is outlined that may confirm this hypothesis.

papers.title: Natural environmental drivers of seagrass degradation: A global systematic review with implications for Indonesia
Coastal and marine ecosystems under climate change ecological and socio-environmental impacts
papers.abstract: Coastal and marine systems are some of the most biologically productive and economically important systems on Earth, yet they are being compromised at an accelerating pace by climate change. Ocean warming, marine heatwaves, sea-level rise, ocean acidification and deoxygenation along with increasing extreme events are interacting to change the structure, function and resilience of ecosystems among coral reefs, mangroves seagrass meadows and salt marshes. Although effort has been devoted to understanding individual ecosystem effects of climatic change, we know less about comparative mechanistic synthesis and cross-ecosystem vulnerability trajectories. This synthesis explores recent understanding of the biophysical determinants of ecosystem decline, with particular reference to thresholds, regime shifts and feedbacks that limit capacity to adapt. We explore different sensitivities among these biogenic coastal systems, and explain why coral reefs are confronted with sharp thermal and carbonate chemistry thresholds, while mangroves and tidal wetlands have threshold-based resilience contingent on sediment supply and geomorphologic setting. Beyond ecological effects, we compile social–environmental responses including fishery reduction, coastal defense loss and blue carbon release, and rising human vulnerability especially in small island and developing coastal regions. The review also examines ecosystem-based adaptation and nature-based solutions, considering their co-benefits and implementation challenges in a high-emission world. By synthesizing climate drivers, ecosystem thresholds, and social–ecological tipping points within a unified conceptual framework, this review integrates mechanisms of change and alternative stable-state transitions to improve understanding of coastal ecosystem resilience under accelerating climate change.

papers.title: Socio-economic drivers and governance failures in the artisanal exploitation of marine turtles along the Mogadishu and Adale Coasts, Somalia
papers.abstract: Empirical data on artisanal marine turtle extraction in Somalia remains exceptionally scarce. This study documents the socio-economic drivers, operational methods, and local perceptions surrounding the illicit capture of marine turtles at artisanal landing sites along the Mogadishu and Adale coasts. Using purposive and snowball sampling, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 25 active artisanal fishermen and 5 institutional informants (N = 30). Respondents described extraction not as incidental bycatch, but a targeted, commercialised activity primarily impacting Green ( Chelonia mydas ) and vulnerable Loggerhead ( Caretta caretta ) turtles. The economic incentive is substantial, with intact turtles commanding up to 120 USD. Demand is heavily influenced by ethnobiological beliefs regarding turtle derivatives treating tuberculosis and asthma—uses unsupported by clinical evidence that expose consumers to chelonitoxism and heavy metal bioaccumulation risks. Reported frequencies are presented as counts of the 25 fishermen respondents with percentages and 95% confidence intervals, and represent recalled self-report from a small non-probability sample rather than verified catch records. Fishers primarily use large-mesh Ildheer gillnets in nearshore seagrass beds. Despite federal prohibitions under the Somali Fisheries Law, local enforcement at artisanal landing sites is functionally absent, mirroring constraints in Somalia’s industrial fisheries. These findings suggest that purely top-down enforcement is insufficient in this fragile governance context. Locally negotiated co-management arrangements, combined with targeted public health messaging regarding the severe toxicological risks of turtle consumption, represent a more viable, evidence-based policy direction.

papers.title: Ammonium uptake plasticity and allocation trade-offs may shape invasion potential of Halophila stipulacea in the Caribbean
papers.abstract: Nutrient uptake traits shape plant competition, yet nutrient acquisition and internal allocation strategies remain poorly resolved for invasive seagrasses, limiting predictions of responses to eutrophication. Over the past two decades, the exotic seagrass Halophila stipulacea has rapidly colonized the Mediterranean and Caribbean, occasionally displacing native species. Competition for inorganic nitrogen, particularly ammonium, may therefore drive future meadow composition and functioning. Using a novel split-chamber incubation system, we compared leaf and root ammonium ( 15 NH 4 + ) uptake kinetics and internal nitrogen transfer among three native Caribbean seagrasses ( Thalassia testudinum, Halodule wrightii, Syringodium filiforme ) and the exotic H. stipulacea. We further synthesized published ammonium uptake and transfer data to contextualize our findings. Leaf uptake exceeded root uptake by nearly an order of magnitude across species. Native species exhibited high root uptake affinity and balanced internal allocation, consistent with nutrient-conservative strategies in oligotrophic enivronments. In contrast, H. stipulacea showed lower root uptake but exceptionally high maximum leaf uptake rates and strong root-to-leaf transfer at elevated ammonium, indicating opportunistic aboveground allocation under nutrient pulses. Some species displayed non-saturating uptake kinetics, suggesting uptake capacity may be underestimated under eutrophic conditions. Our synthesis revealed substantial inter- and intraspecific variability and showed 80% of seagrass species lack kinetic parameters. Native Caribbean seagrasses are likely competitively favoured under low to moderate ammonium concentrations, whereas H. stipulacea may gain a context-dependent advantage under nutrient enrichment. These findings illustrate how trade-offs between nutrient-use efficiency and flexibility shape invasion potential highlight critical mechanistic data gaps for predicting future seagrass dominance and ecosystem functioning.

papers.title: Genome-wide sequencing of clonal seagrass reveals high heterozygosity and low genetic structure in the Western Mediterranean
papers.abstract: Abstract Posidonia oceanica is a keystone Mediterranean seagrass whose clonality, episodic sexual recruitment, and slow growth constrain adaptation to environmental change. We generated whole-genome resequencing data for 24 individuals from the Balearic Islands and nearby western Mediterranean localities and analyzed ~25 million variants (1.30 million SNPs after linkage disequilibrium pruning) to characterize genome-wide diversity, relatedness, and structure. SNP density and nucleotide diversity (π ≈ 0.00011 in 50-kb windows) were broadly uniform across chromosomes and highly concordant, indicating no strong sweep-like signatures at the sampled scale. Tajima's D was frequently positive (often >2), and inbreeding coefficients were negative for most samples, revealing excess heterozygosity consistent with divergent haplotypes within long-lived clones. Kinship estimates showed that many genotypes were second- to third-degree relatives despite wide geographic separation, including one first-degree pair (CHA2-MAL4), suggesting historical dispersal followed by long-term clonal persistence. Spatial ancestry inference favored a one-ancestry-cluster solution (K = 1), although models with K = 2-3 revealed a subtle east-west gradient and a distinct Alborán component; a maximum-likelihood tree recovered an eastern clade sister to the remaining samples and a monophyletic Alborán subclade within western lineages. Together, these results show that Balearic P. oceanica meadows combine exceptional clonal longevity with high genome-wide heterozygosity and occupy a central position within a weak but detectable west-to-east cline. These findings highlight how clonality and rare sex can maintain standing genetic variation over millennial timescales despite limited contemporary gene flow.

papers.title: Valorization of Posidonia oceanica balls: sustainable simultaneous synthesis of green de-icer and eco-friendly adsorbent for saline water treatment from methylene blue
papers.abstract: Abstract Neptune beach balls (NB) are natural waste materials often found along the Mediterranean Sea coasts. NB are originated from the decay of Posidonia oceanica (PO) organs leaving balls of the plant fibers, sand and impurities. Due to upcoming global warming, the accumulation of contaminants-loaded NB among PO wastes, they are expected to intensify, increasing the environmental challenges posed by these eco-wastes. This study presents a novelle sustainable acetic-acid activation strategy for the double valorization of Neptune balls (NB) into an eco-friendly adsorbent and green deicer. The materials were characterized using ICP-OES, FTIR, Raman spectroscopy, XRD, TGA, SEM-EDX, zeta potential, and/or pH PZC analyses. Through a simple and economical treatment process, 84.5% of the cleaned NB waste is transformed into a natural adsorbent. Simultaneously, the circular economy is approached by valorizing the acid activation liquor waste into an environmentally friendly calcium magnesium acetate (CMA) deicer that was recovered with approximately 83% efficiency, as a by-product adding value to the NB valorization process. The natural adsorbent was capable of removing up to 97.5% of MB from freshwater and saline water, with a monolayer MB adsorption capacity of 135 mg g − 1 . The MB adsorption is well fitted by the Langmuir and Freundlich models while following the pseudo-second-order kinetics model. MB-multilayer was suggested to be adsorbed primarily by electrostatic attraction. The activated NB has been successfully tested for the removal of MB dye from seawater spiked with MB, while CMA demonstrated better deicing performance compared to conventional sodium chloride salt, highlighting the potential to advance the economic valorization of NB waste, supporting both water treatment and eco-waste management.

papers.title: Mediterranean Posidonia blue-carbon prioritisation under maritime pressure; code and data
papers.abstract: Full analysis chain and gridded dataset for a GIS-MCDM prioritisation of Posidonia oceanica blue-carbon conservation and restoration in the western–central Mediterranean under maritime traffic and anchoring pressure. Includes: (1) Colab notebooks that assemble a 90,000-cell 0.05° grid from open EMODnet, Marine Regions and MAPAMED layers and enrich it with EEZ jurisdiction, areal-intersection MPA membership and zonal bathymetry statistics; (2) a self-contained Python script that reproduces, from the included art45_grid_v5.csv, every statistic and figure reported in the associated manuscript — CRITIC weighting, value–pressure decoupling, conflict typology, the jurisdictional governance gap, depth-validated robustness checks, weighting- and aggregator-sensitivity, anchoring-proxy sensitivity, and the permutation test of conservation–restoration separation. Fixed seeds; no network access needed for reproduction.

papers.title: Territorial environmental transformations: GIS and remote sensing for monitoring sustainable coastal landscapes
papers.abstract: Abstract Coastal landscapes are critical territorial assets increasingly threatened by climate-driven processes such as erosion, salinisation, and habitat loss, requiring integrated monitoring frameworks that combine GIS, remote sensing, and local education. This study adapts the Elittoral methodology—originally developed for French coastal diagnostics—by integrating participatory GIS and Sentinel satellite imagery to support sustainable coastal governance in Mediterranean and Atlantic contexts. Methods include multi-temporal analyses (2015–2025) using Sentinel-2 data to assess shoreline change (DSAS), land-cover dynamics (NDVI/NDWI), and bathymetric variation (ICESat-2). QGIS workflows incorporate citizen-generated data (beach profiles, Posidonia meadows, urban encroachment) and are calibrated against Elittoral protocols. Educational modules engage students through photogrammetry and mobile GIS, co-producing vulnerability maps for municipal ICZM plans. Random Forest classification distinguishes anthropogenic from natural changes, validated with ground-truth data (Kappa > 85%). Results show contrasting dynamics: Mediterranean coasts exhibit 1.5–2.5 m/year erosion linked to tourism pressure, while Atlantic dunes gain + 15% through managed realignment. Salinisation fronts advance up to 500 m inland, and citizen science improves microplastic detection (+ 40%). Educational initiatives increase risk awareness (+ 55%) and civic engagement. The study highlights hybrid monitoring as both scientific and pedagogical, supporting resilient and participatory coastal management despite ongoing data governance challenges.

papers.title: 2018-2019 The Brothers Island Vascular Plant Botanical Inventory
papers.abstract: 2018-2019 The Brothers Islands Vascular Plant Botanical Inventory Knox County, Saint George, Maine, United States.The Brothers Islands (CIR: 63-579 & 63-581)The Brothers Islands are along the mid-coast of Maine off of Port Clyde. Inventory Conducted: There were 5 separate trips to the island between June and September (Aug. 9, 2018, Aug. 21, 2018, 15 Sep. 2018, Jun. 19, 2019, Jul. 16, 2019). Maine Natural History ObservatoryLead Botanist: Glen MittelhauserContact: info@mainenaturalhistory.orgFunding Sources: Maine Coastal Islands National Wildlife Refuge -----------------------------Permissions and Data Use These data are made publicly available to encourage transparency, long-term preservation, and reuse in ecological research, conservation planning, and education. These inventories represent baseline conditions at the time of survey and should be interpreted with appropriate consideration of survey year, methods, and observer effort. Users are welcome to download, analyze, and incorporate these data into derivative works, including independent analyses and publications. Any use of these data must acknowledge the original source by citing the website where the data are archived and giving credit for the historical data to Glen Mittelhauser, Maine Natural History Observatory. Users are encouraged, though not required, to notify Maine Natural History Observatory of substantial or interpretive uses of the dataset, particularly those leading to publication. -----------------------------File list and description of each file(See report for more information) 1) Core fileFile Name: TheBrothersIslands2018-2019_EventCore_GridCells.csv Description: Using GIS software, we built a 25x25 m grid across the island with a total of 88 grid cells that had at least some vascular plants. The grid was oriented following true compass bearings, with the UTM coordinates (NAD83, Zone 19) of the grid extent being 480550, 4862275 and 480950, 4861775.This file contains coordinates only for the grid cells that contained vascular plants. GRID CELLS2) Extension of Core fileFile Name: TheBrothersIslands2018-2019_Occurrences_GridCells.csv Connects to: TheBrothersIslands2018-2019_EventCore_GridCells.csv linked using the gridCell column. Description: On each trip to the island, we visited all grid cells, made a list of vascular plants present within each grid cell, and estimated the categorical abundance of each. Abundance categories were as follows: common = species with a wide distribution in the grid cell, occurring in large numbers, typically with over 50% cover; occasional = species with a scattered distribution throughout the grid cell, typically with 25-50% cover; uncommon = species not widely distributed and not often encountered in the grid cell, typically with 5-25% cover; and rare = species usually restricted to small areas, specialized habitats, or consisting of 1 or 2 very small "populations" in the grid cell, typically with less than 5% cover. By comparing species abundances within grid cells on the various trips, we documented the maximum categorical abundance of each species in each grid cell on the islands. QUADRATS3) Extension of Core fileFile Name: TheBrothersIslands2018-2019_Quadrats.csv Connects to: TheBrothersIslands2018-2019_EventCore_GridCells.csv linked using the gridCell column. Description: Within a subset of selected grid cells with vascular plants present, we also estimated cover of each species within 1x1 m quadrats to measure the vegetation in the interior of the island. For measuring the vegetation in the interior of the island (13 grid cells), the location of the 1x1 m quadrats was based off of the center of each selected 25x25 m grid cell (estimated with the GPS unit), with three quadrats placed approximately 2 m from the center of the grid cell: one quadrat 2 m to the N, one quadrat 2 m to the SE, and one quadrat 2 m to the SW. If trampled vegetation was in the quadrat location, the quadrat was tossed further from the center point of the grid cell. Because many species in the island interior matured earlier in the season, we conducted these surveys during July before most of the interior vegetation dried up.Each 1x1 m vegetation sampling quadrat was sampled non-destructively for visual estimates of cover for each species of vascular plants, with separate categories recorded for rock, dead vegetation, bare soil, and washed up debris near the shore. Plant cover was estimated as accurately as possible, without rounding to categories or even the nearest percent, especially when considering rare species. We used calibration templates showing 1 %, 2.5%, and 5% cover and negative-space templates for 0.5% and 1% cover to help with cover estimates. We also carried transparent templates for fractions of cover from 0.1% to 1% for various size rectangles, ellipses, and circles. When estimating cover, we ignored small gaps between leaflets of compound leaves, but larger and important gaps between leaves were considered. The two belt transects were located to be evenly spaced within the grid cell. papers.title: The sound of resilience? Exploring trophic cascades and positive feedbacks between cod and eelgrass in a trawl-free ecosystem
papers.abstract: This study examines The Sound, a strait between Denmark and Sweden protected by a trawl ban since 1932. Consistent with previous research, we show that the area supports greater densities, sizes, and landings of Atlantic cod (Gadus morhua) than adjacent trawled waters. Simulations from a bespoke food web model indicate that predation from the cod can suppress mesopredators, thus reducing filamentous algal growth through a trophic cascade, which benefits eelgrass (Zostera marina). In line with this, monitoring data show lower mesopredator densities and more extensive eelgrass meadows in The Sound compared with nearby trawled areas, although salinity and hydrodynamic conditions could also contribute. However, despite the trawl ban, adult cod densities are currently at their lowest levels since monitoring started, raising concerns about the ecosystem's long-term resilience. Model results further demonstrate how preserving eelgrass meadows benefits cod, illustrating feedback mechanisms that highlight the importance of integrated fisheries and conservation management.

papers.title: Location and habitat specificity structure benthic microbial assemblages in a temperate seagrass ecosystem
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Seagrass meadows are globally distributed coastal ecosystems that provide habitats for diverse species and facilitate ecosystem services, such as carbon storage and nutrient cycling. However, anthropogenic activities and climate change are causing seagrass decline worldwide, broadly impacting ecosystem functioning. Although macrofaunal communities in seagrass habitats are relatively well studied, benthic microbial assemblages (including microeukaryote groups such as protists and microbial metazoa) remain underexplored. In this study, we used environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding to characterize assemblages of bacteria/archaea (16S rRNA gene), microeukaryotes (18S rRNA amplified from raw sediment), and meiofauna (18S rRNA amplified from sieved and Ludoxed sediment fractions) in seagrass fields and bare sediment habitats at three sites along an estuarine gradient in Bodega Harbor, California. We found that microbial and microeukaryote communities were primarily structured by location, with sediment properties (sand vs silt/clay proportions) being the main driver of community assemblages. Habitat type was a secondary factor influencing benthic fauna, with bare sediments typically displaying higher biodiversity than seagrass beds, except at Westside Park mudflats, where bare sediments showed significantly reduced diversity compared to all other sampling locations. The differential recovery of nematode bioindicator taxa, including Terschellingia, Daptonema, Viscosia, Microlaimus, and Spilophorella, suggested that abiotic factors, such as physical disturbance, pollution, or oxygen dynamics, may influence the success of specific taxa at each site. Finally, nematode-bacterial co-occurrence networks confirmed known symbiotic associations and suggest additional taxonomic relationships to explore in future studies. Our findings underscore the importance of environmental gradients and microhabitat features in shaping benthic biodiversity in temperate seagrass ecosystems. IMPORTANCE Seagrass meadows, which sustain a wide variety of plant and animal life, are vital coastal habitats. These submerged ecosystems support biodiversity, coastal protection, biogeochemical cycling, and carbon storage. However, seagrass habitats worldwide are declining due to pressures from climate change and human activity. This study characterizes the microbial and microeukaryote communities (including microbial animals with a body size <1 mm) that inhabit and surround temperate seagrass meadows in Bodega Harbor, California. Our findings demonstrate that location is a primary factor that determines microbial communities inhabiting sediments at each site, with habitat type (bare sediment vs seagrass beds) exerting a secondary influence on the biodiversity and distribution of microbial species. By using nematode bioindicator taxa and nematode-bacterial co-occurrence patterns, our results also suggest specific environmental factors that shape sediment biodiversity, including tidal cycles, oxygen, sulfur, and decaying organic matter. A comprehensive understanding of the variation within benthic communities associated with seagrass habitats can significantly enhance conservation and restoration efforts for seagrass meadows. papers.title: Abundance and Size of Seagrass-Associated Fishes in the Virginia Coastal Lagoons, 2019-2026
papers.abstract: These data comprise annual summer estimates of the abundance (counts) and size (length) of fishes across restored seagrass meadows of the Virginia coastal lagoons. Fish were collected using a 25-ft (7.62-m) wide beach seine hauled by hand over a 25 m linear swath of the seafloor. Seine hauls were collected in June at 31 sites (1 haul per site). All fish caught in the seine were identified to lowest practical taxonomic level, counted, measured (total length), and released. Data collection began in June 2019 and continues annually (sampling was not carried out in 2020 due to logistical interruptions associated with the COVID-19 pandemic). Data on water temperature, salinity, and conductivity were collected while sampling occurred using a YSI 30 probe. Dissolved oxygen measurements were collected using a YSI ProODO probe. In 2019, these data were collected on at the top and bottom of the water column, but in 2021 and subsequent sampling only one observation (mid-water column) was made. To reconcile this difference for the combined data set, top and bottom environmental measurements from 2019 were averaged. Each fish collection site is co-located with a nearby synoptic site where long-term measurements of seagrass, sediments, and fauna are made. The relationship between site names and coordinates are given in Synoptic_fish_sites.csv. The sites where fish sampling occurred are different and are given by the "fish_sites" column, with coordinates for these sites under the "fish_longitude" and "fish_latitude" columns. Importantly, the coordinates of where sampling occurred will differ slightly between years without a change to the name of the site. Site geographic coordinates for individual years are in the PhysicalSamples.csv file. Sites are separated by at least 300 meters. In 2023, three new sites were added to represent unvegetated areas outside of but near the seagrass meadows. These sites are HI29, SPDR-bare, and SS-bare, and are designed to serve as references for seagrass sites in Hog Island Bay, Spider Crab Bay / Cobb Bay, and South Bay / Ship Shoal, respectively. Note: related but methodologically different data for 2012-2018 are available in dataset VCR14232 "Fish Counts and Lengths in South Bay and Hog Island Bay, Virginia 2012-2018" https://doi.org/10.6073/pasta/cae6c1c3f90b1f7d65ec0c1ae9b94398

papers.title: Mapping offshore wind potential and spatial trade-offs for marine planning in Caribbean Small Island Developing States
papers.abstract: Offshore wind is a prominent strategic option for decarbonizing power systems and enhancing energy security in Small Island Developing States (SIDS). However, its strategic implementation in the Caribbean is hindered by fragmented spatial data concerning resource availability, technological feasibility, and multi-sectoral trade-offs. This study establishes a reproducible, marine-planning-oriented spatial screening framework that synthesizes wind resource climatologies with critical environmental constraints to delineate opportunity and trade-off zones across the Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZs) of 12 Caribbean SIDS. We first mapped wind speeds at 100 m and integrated country-level technical potentials, including fixed-bottom and floating offshore foundation technologies to facilitate an integrated cross-jurisdictional assessment. A multi-criteria conflict index was subsequently developed from spatial datasets representing Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) and sensitive benthic habitats, specifically coral reefs and seagrass meadows. Our spatial analysis identifies 10.03% of the maritime domain as ‘Opportunity’ zones—areas where high wind resources align with low ecological and jurisdictional constraints. Significantly, ‘Trade-off’ zones occupy only 0.36% of the region, revealing a pronounced spatial decoupling between peak wind resources and existing ecological protections. Conversely, 14.88% of the area is classified as ‘Avoid’ zones, predominantly concentrated in nearshore environments. By integrating resource potential, foundation technologies, and constraint layers into a transparent workflow, this study provides a rigorous evidence base to transition from national-level aggregates to actionable, sub-EEZ siting strategies in the Caribbean.

papers.title: Effects of blue carbon restoration strategies on sediment carbon sinks and underlying mechanisms across contrasting hydrogeomorphic settings.
papers.abstract: Blue carbon ecosystems contain disproportionately large carbon stocks and have therefore become priority targets for ecological restoration. Yet long-term effectiveness of restoration remains uncertain because species choice and hydrogeomorphic settings are rarely evaluated together in relation to carbon sequestration. Here, we analyzed sediment C and N accumulation in 90 cores from natural and restored mangroves, seagrass beds, and tidal flats across estuarine and open-coast settings in South China, integrating multi-decadal dating, stable-isotopic analysis, and an organic matter diagenetic model to improve comparisons of historical C and N inputs. Our results suggest that natural mangroves were the principal sedimentary C and N reservoirs, exhibiting the highest burials and stocks. However, restoration effects on C and N burial were strongly context dependent. Specifically, native-species restoration outperformed exotic-species in large-river estuaries, whereas exotic-species restoration outpaced native-species restoration in open-coast and small-river estuarine mangroves. Nevertheless, exotic-restored stands in coastal mangroves showed lower apparent stability of organic matter despite high burial rates. Restored seagrass meadows had C and N burial rates comparable to natural meadows. Decadal dating and δ 13 C SOC profiles indicated that hydrogeomorphic setting and restoration strategy shaped temporal trajectories of C and N inputs. Structural equation modelling further identified vegetation type and factors associated with hydrogeomorphic setting, including position, sedimentation rate, and porewater chemistry, as key controls on C and N stocks. Together, these results highlight that restoration planning should begin with an assessment of hydrogeomorphic conditions to guide restoration priorities, thereby strengthening the climate credibility of blue carbon restoration.

papers.title: Editorial: Rising stars in remote sensing 2025: advancements in time series analysis
papers.abstract: A central theme across the collection is the movement from mapping change to diagnosing response trajectories. In ["Recording seagrass growth in Mosquito Lagoon, Florida after Hurricanes Ian and Nicole"], Insalaco et al. use semi-monthly Harmonized Landsat-Sentinel imagery and Random Forest classification to examine rapid seagrass recovery following two major hurricanes in 2022. Their work shows the value of dense temporal monitoring for capturing ecological responses that would be difficult to interpret from isolated pre-and post-event imagery. The study documents a striking post-disturbance trajectory: seagrass remained limited into early 2023 but recovered to pre-collapse levels by summer 2023, raising important questions about disturbance, recovery, water quality, and coastal ecosystem resilience.Disturbance detection is also central to ["Mapping small-scale logging disturbances in tropical forests using Sentinel-1 time series and an extensive ground truth dataset"], where Mercier et al. address one of the persistent challenges in tropical forest monitoring: identifying small-scale forest degradation that may remain invisible in global forest-cover products. Using dense Sentinel-1 SAR time series, extensive treefelling records, and UAV-borne lidar data, the authors develop and evaluate approaches for detecting very small logging disturbances in the Congo Basin. Their Fused-Lasso Change Detection approach represents the clearest methodological innovation in the collection, showing how radar time series can help overcome cloud-cover limitations and improve detection of subtle, short-lived forest disturbances, especially where selective and artisanal logging create canopy gaps much smaller than conventional monitoring thresholds.The collection also demonstrates the importance of long-term time series for monitoring hydrological change. In ["Monitoring the dual-season hydrological dynamics of the Pong reservoir in Himachal Pradesh, India"], Sarda and Kumar use three decades of Landsat imagery to evaluate pre-and postmonsoon reservoir dynamics. By comparing water indices, hydrological consistency, and relative water depth, the study identifies seasonal and multi-decadal changes in the Pong Reservoir, an important Ramsar site. MNDWI proved effective for mapping reservoir water cover, and areas of high hydrological consistency declined substantially in the pre-monsoon season. This work illustrates how established spectral-index approaches, when applied consistently through time, can provide useful information for conservation planning, water-resource management, and monitoring of human-modified aquatic systems. The broader conceptual significance of these applied studies is developed in ["Terrestrial ecosystems are in transition"]. Wang et al. synthesize evidence that climate change, land-use change, altered disturbance regimes, and biogeochemical imbalances are eroding ecosystem resilience and increasing the risk of critical transitions. Their review emphasizes the importance of remote sensing time series for detecting early-warning signals, monitoring vegetation dynamics, and identifying ecosystems approaching thresholds. In doing so, the article provides a wider framework for interpreting the other contributions in this Research Topic: time series remote sensing is not only a mapping tool, but also a means of diagnosing resilience, vulnerability, and possible transition pathways.Taken together, the articles in this Research Topic show the diversity of questions now being addressed through remote sensing time series analysis (Figure 1). They span marine and coastal vegetation recovery, tropical forest degradation, reservoir hydrology, dryland vegetation monitoring, and ecosystem transition theory. Most contributions apply well-established tools, including machine learning classification, spectral water and vegetation indices, pixel-based trend analysis, and multi-decadal image archives. Their value lies in applying these approaches to environmental systems where timing, persistence, and spatial heterogeneity matter. At the same time, Mercier et al.'s radar time-series analysis points toward the need for further algorithmic development for difficult monitoring problems, including cloud-prone environments, small disturbances, mixed pixels, and rapidly changing landscape features.Several cross-cutting lessons emerge from the collection. First, disturbance detection depends strongly on sensor choice and temporal density: optical time series are powerful for tracking vegetation and water dynamics, while SAR offers key advantages where clouds or canopy structure limit optical observation. Second, validation remains a central challenge. High-resolution UAV, lidar, field, and imageinterpretation datasets can build confidence at local scales, but applying methods to coarser global products or to regions without detailed ground data remains difficult. Third, many studies can diagnose what changed, when, and where, but the attribution of drivers-such as rainfall variability, water quality, land management, grazing, sedimentation, or human activity-remains a major frontier.The work highlighted here points toward three priorities for the field: integrating AI and time series methods with ecological theory, bridging scale gaps between local validation and regional or global products, and expanding robust monitoring approaches in data-limited regions, including much of the Global South. This Research Topic therefore celebrates a set of strong individual contributions while also identifying broader challenges for the emerging generation of remote sensing scientists. As satellite archives lengthen, revisit times improve, and analytical methods continue to advance, remote sensing time series will play an increasingly central role in diagnosing environmental response trajectories and supporting timely, spatially explicit decisions for conservation, restoration, water-resource management, and climate adaptation.

papers.title: The tenth anniversary of the first invasive seaweed of European Union concern: Rugulopteryx okamurae
papers.abstract: Although there were indications of its presence in the Strait of Gibraltar in 2015, it was not until 2016 that the identity and presence of the brown seaweed was confirmed on the coast of Ceuta in northern Africa (Spain) (Altamirano et al. 2016). This species, which is native to the western Pacific, was first detected on the French Mediterranean coast in 2002. However, it did not begin to exhibit invasive behaviour until it arrived in southern Spain. Over the past ten years, it has spread to the coasts of Portugal, France, Italy, Morocco, Algeria, Spain, and the Macaronesia islands. The ecological and socio-economic impacts of this species are unprecedented, justifying its designation as a species of special concern for the Union. This makes it the first marine macroalgae species to be classified as such. This presentation will share information on these impacts, particularly on rocky seabeds and seagrass beds, where drastic biodiversity loss has occurred. It will also address the impacts on the fishing industry and local councils regarding the removal of seaweed, which results in millions of euros in losses each year. The presentation will also address key aspects of the species' invasiveness outside its native range, focusing particularly on its vegetative phenology (morpho-anatomical changes and population dynamics) (Rosas-Guerrero et al. 2025), and its reproductive phenology (Rosas-Guerrero et al. 2026). Notably, the species has an enormous capacity to produce numerous new individuals through clonal mechanisms. These individuals attach themselves not only to the seabed but also grow in the water column. It has been estimated that the pressure exerted by propagules exceeds the carrying capacity of the marine substrate, with more than half a million potential new individuals invading Posidonia oceanica per m² per year. At a physiological level, R. okamurae exhibits a high capacity to acclimatise to changing light conditions. This enables it to live at different depths and survive in darkness for extended periods without losing viability (Rosas‐Guerrero et al. 2025). For this reason, managing R. okamurae poses significant challenges at local, regional, national and international levels. Mitigating its impacts requires coordination among the relevant authorities, who must establish measures to monitor and prevent further introductions and dispersal, as well as implement strategies to manage the biomass it produces — all within the current regulatory framework. Currently, R. okamurae continues to expand its range, causing impacts wherever it arrives. If the predictive models developed for this species are accurate, it could represent the most severe invasion of the European marine environment to date, threatening the resilience of our marine habitats.

papers.title: Ecosystem health of Scottish seagrass meadows: current status and future monitoring approaches
papers.abstract: Temperate seagrass meadows are biodiverse habitats that form a key part of coastal seascapes and provide a unique suite of ecosystem services. However, seagrass has declined dramatically globally and in the UK over the last century, with knock-on effects for the provision of these services as well as the functioning of the wider food web. Understanding of the health status of meadows in Scotland is limited both in geographic coverage and in the breadth of ecosystem health metrics assessed, hindering our ability to prioritise conservation measures, and tailor them to the needs of individual meadows. There is therefore a clear need for expanded assessments of seagrass ecosystem health in Scotland. To achieve this, monitoring approaches need to be scalable and practicable for a range of stakeholders, including local communities, who play a central role in marine conservation and monitoring in Scotland. This thesis addresses this need with two aims: 1) enhancing understanding of ecosystem health of subtidal and intertidal seagrass meadows in Scotland, in geographic coverage and breadth of metrics assessed; and 2) evaluating a set of robust, socially inclusive metrics of seagrass ecosystem health to improve monitoring strategies. This was achieved through field-based assessments of ecosystem health across three subtidal and three intertidal meadows, using indicators spanning: vegetation composition and structure, abiotic conditions (including nutrient enrichment proxies), motile aquatic fauna (fish and decapods), and use of meadows by semi-aquatic fauna (birds, otters and seals). Metrics were chosen to maximise taxonomic breadth and functional relevance, capturing structural complexity, trophic interactions and indications of ecological resilience. Modifications to methods suitable for community-led projects were explored, and two novel monitoring approaches were trialled: remote video footage for studying semi-aquatic fauna, and passive acoustic monitoring for motile aquatic fauna. Established ecological theory was used to inform selection of metrics and interpretation of how they reflect ecosystem health. Chapter 1 provides a review of the urgent case for seagrass protection and restoration in Scotland, why understanding of ecosystem health is crucial for successful conservation practice, and the gaps in this understanding. The term ecosystem health, how it relates to biodiversity, and how it translates into measurable parameters for a temperate seagrass meadow are discussed, providing a platform for the aims and objectives of the thesis. Chapter 2 introduces the field sites and the data collected at each. Context is provided on the geomorphological features and anthropogenic impacts at each site, as well as features of the study design that affect interpretation of results. Chapter 3 characterises the vegetative and abiotic components of ecosystem health across each meadow. Of concern is the continued decline of intertidal seagrass at Loch Fleet in Sutherland, and identification of nutrient enrichment as a likely driver of this. There were indications of poor water quality and/or competition from macroalgae posing a risk to meadow health at all sites, although the strength of this evidence varied. Substantial variation in seagrass and macroalgal density also sets the scene for the following chapters, by identifying potential drivers of faunal community composition as well as mechanisms that may confound assessments of the faunal community. Chapter 4 quantifies the motile aquatic faunal communities of the subtidal meadows. Substantial variation was identified among sites, with one meadow – on the Isle of Skye – emerging as exceptionally diverse for fish and decapods, and an abundance of higher trophic level fish taxa suggesting a greater intactness of ecosystem functions. Seagrass was found to be associated with greater gadoid and wrasse abundance, compared to sand-macroalgae mosaic controls, suggesting that these meadows were fulfilling their function as a fish nursery. Chapter 5 broadens the scope of standard ecosystem health assessments by including semi-aquatic fauna that only transiently visit meadows. A range of both predatory and herbivorous birds and predatory mammals were documented feeding in seagrass. In the intertidal (controlling for tidal stage), waders, gulls and dabbling ducks/geese showed a preference for feeding in seagrass over control mudflat, with the most robust evidence for curlew and oystercatcher. A novel survey method – remote video of the water surface – was developed and trialled, which provided the first quantification of otter and shag feeding behaviour in subtidal meadows. Chapter 6 explores another novel method: passive acoustic monitoring for assessing diversity of motile aquatic fauna. Phonic richness – the number of different types of sounds – in the low-frequency band (the range in which sounds made by fish typically fall), was found to correlate with visual measures of fish diversity, demonstrating the potential of this approach as an efficient monitoring tool. Acoustic indices – which summarise characteristics of the soundscape – were found to be less reliable as indicators of faunal diversity, and their use is cautioned against for this habitat. Chapter 7 summarises the thesis findings on the ecosystem health of each meadow, key drivers of different metrics, and evaluation of monitoring approaches. Recommendations are made for the development of monitoring strategies led by a range of stakeholders, alongside discussion of implications for policy. Throughout the thesis, I explore two cross-cutting themes: the effects of seagrass presence on metrics of ecosystem health, and relationships between different health metrics. Overall, seagrass presence was found to have a weaker effect than site identity on metric values, with additional extrinsic factors having major driving effects on some metrics: tidal stage for intertidal bird feeding behaviour, and time of day for acoustic activity. This highlights the importance of controlling for such factors in ecosystem health assessments, including considering the interdependence of faunal communities among neighbouring habitats in a seascape. Investigating the relationship between metrics revealed that higher seagrass density was not necessarily associated with higher faunal diversity. While ecological theory predicts a positive relationship between habitat complexity and biodiversity, results suggest that this relationship may be non-linear or context dependent. There was evidence that such non-linearity may in part be caused by vegetation having a confounding effect on both visual and acoustic surveys, by preventing the transmission of visual and acoustic information, as well as producing ‘popping’ sounds from photosynthesis which may mask the identification of target faunal sounds. The strengths and weaknesses of each monitoring method are discussed, and potential refinements to established methods suggested, in the context of suitability for community groups and other users. The rapid advancement of machine learning is recognised as a key factor in unlocking the full potential of both video- and audio-based monitoring methods, increasing both their efficiency and accessibility to a wider user group. In response, I highlight the need for standardisation and to account for key confounding factors – namely transmission loss and masking – to ensure that an increased volume of data collection and analysis generates reliable and informative results. Overall, this thesis expands understanding of seagrass meadow health in Scotland, demonstrating that the faunal biodiversity they support can be exceptionally high whilst also highlighting declines at one site and widespread risks to health. It identifies opportunities to refine established monitoring methods, as well as revealing the potential of novel methods: further development of remote video could permit semi-aquatic fauna to act as indicators of meadow health, and advances in passive acoustic monitoring could complement visual approaches to monitoring fish. These findings can guide restoration targets, justify investment in seagrass conservation, inform the placement and approach of protection and restoration efforts, and influence the design of monitoring strategies that are efficient, accurate and inclusive. In this way, this thesis supports the long-term conservation of seagrass meadows, and their rich array of values, in Scotland and beyond.

papers.title: Transplanting Seagrass Plants into Nursery Raceways v1
papers.abstract: This protocol describes methods for transplanting adult seagrass plants into laboratory nursery tanks following collection from field sites. Steps describe the preparation of planting pots, sediments or other substrate to be used for growing plants, and physically transplanting individual seagrass plants into the newly prepared substrate, as well as labeling individual plants if they are to be tracked through a research experiment.

papers.title: Shoot Structure and Leaf Morphometry Measurements for Seagrass Nursery Plants v1
papers.abstract: This protocol describes methods for measuring leaf length and leaf width and counting the number of leaves on seagrass plants growing within laboratory nursery tanks. Steps describe counting the number of leaves and shoots on plants growing within individual planting pots, and measuring leaf length and leaf width on individual plants using a ruler directly within nursery tanks.

papers.title: Protocols for the collection, transplantation, and rearing of adult seagrass plants within land-based nurseries for research purposes v1
papers.abstract: This collection contains protocols related to various aspects of growing and using seagrass plants in controlled nursery settings for research purposes. These protocols were developed for a research project as part of Florida’s Seagrass Restoration Technology Development Initiative funded by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection and Mote Marine Laboratory. Protocols are provided for the collection of seagrass plants from natural meadows, transplantation of seagrass plants into nursery tanks, measurement of seagrass leaf characteristics within nursery tanks, adding nutrients directly to sediment substrates for seagrass growth, collecting research samples of sediment porewater, and harvesting of seagrass plants from nursery tanks for subsequent analyses.

papers.title: Satellite-based total suspended matter as an indicator of coastal surface blue-carbon distribution: a case study of two bays in Japan
papers.abstract: Coastal blue-carbon ecosystems, particularly seagrass meadows, play a disproportionate role in global carbon sequestration. However, the spatial distribution of exported particulate organic matter (POM) remains poorly understood at large spatial scales. Satellite remote sensing offers a promising approach for monitoring coastal carbon dynamics, yet most studies have focused on benthic seagrass distribution rather than suspended carbon in the water column. This study evaluated the potential of total suspended matter (TSM) estimated from Global Change Observation Mission-Climate (GCOM-C) observations as a proxy for coastal blue-carbon distribution. Using 250-m gridded data from Sagami Bay and Suruga Bay, Japan, we examined whether TSM reflected POM distribution by testing its relationships with distance from river estuaries and mapped seagrass meadows. TSM showed a significant negative relationship with distance from river estuaries in both bays, consistent with riverine POM inputs. TSM values were also significantly higher within seagrass meadows than in surrounding waters, suggesting that TSM reflects both seagrass-derived organic particles and suspended particles retained within seagrass meadows that may potentially be buried and sequestered. Although TSM integrates both autochthonous and allochthonous material, our results demonstrate that satellite-based TSM provides a feasible, scalable proxy for coastal blue-carbon distribution, supporting future large-scale monitoring and assessment of coastal blue carbon.

papers.title: Features of the specific, spatial, and trophic structure of macrobenthos communities in the lagoon ecosystem of the inner area of the Kislaya Bay (Kandalaksha Gulf, White Sea)
papers.abstract: Features of the specific, spatial and trophic structure of macrobenthos communities in a lagoon ecosystem located at the outlet of the inner area of the Kislaya Bay (Kandalaksha Gulf, White Sea) were studied. 35 species of benthic invertebrates, as well as 9 ones of seagrasses and algae, were found in the lagoon. In it, there is a well–marked vertical gradient in the macrobenthos community structure (from the upper littoral to the middle, lower, and sublittoral) and a less pronounced longitudinal one, from more silty and desalinated coastal habitats to marine ones. Our statistical analysis made it possible to identify a sublittoral macrobenthos (dominated by Macoma balthica mollusks and polychaetes Terebellides stroemi, Nereimyra punctatata, Pontoporeia femorata, Scoloplos armiger, Phyllodoce maculata ), a community of macrobenthos of the lower and middle littoral, dominated by Macoma balthica, Mya arenaria (more in the middle littoral), Arenicola marina, Littorina littorea and Mytilus edulis (more in the lower littoral) and the macrobenthos community of the upper littoral, together with the inner district middle littoral, dominated by small eurytopic species Peringia ulvae, Tubificoides benedii and Littorina saxatilis . In the lagoon, due to its shallow waters, isolation from the sea, predominance of silt-sand sediments and some freshening, mainly detritiphages predominate; their percentage decreases in the middle and lower littoral and increases towards the sublittoral and upper littoral.

papers.title: Macroalgas en praderas mixtas de Thalassia testudinum y Halophila stipulacea en el archipiélago Los Roques, Venezuela
papers.abstract: RESUMEN: Las macroalgas son componentes esenciales en las comunidades de pastos marinos, púes incrementan la biodiversidad y la complejidad estructural del hábitat. En mayo de 2023, se recolectaron muestras de macroalgas en cayo Franciski Abajo (Parque Nacional Archipiélago Los Roques, Venezuela), en una pradera mixta de Thalassia testudinum y Halophila stipulacea, ubicada en un sector somero bordeado por manglares. Los especímenes fueron preservados en formalina al 4% e identificados mediante microscopía estereoscópica y claves taxonómicas. Se registraron 29 especies de macroalgas (16 Rhodophyta, 11 Chlorophyta y 2 Ochrophyta), y dos cianobacterias filamentosas. Nueve especies de macroalgas se encontraron como epífitas en ambas fanerógamas y 20 crecían sobre el sustrato. Se destacó la presencia de costras calcáreas de Hydrolithon farinosum, alga roja que facilita el establecimiento de otros organismos. Asimismo, se observaron evidencias de herbivoría (mordeduras y perforaciones) en las hojas de ambas plantas. H. stipulacea, originaria del Océano Índico, mostró un crecimiento masivo, ocupando los espacios disponibles del sustrato. Los indicios de pastoreo sugieren su integración en la cadena trófica local como productor primario, de manera similar a T. testudinum. Por su parte, la presencia de epífitas en ambos pastos demuestra que el pasto marino exótico cumple un rol ecológico análogo al pasto nativo como sustrato para otros organismos. ABSTRACT: Macroalgae are essential components of seagrass communities, as they increase biodiversity and the structural complexity of the habitat. In May 2023, macroalgae samples were collected at Franciski Abajo Cay (Archipiélago Los Roques National Park, Venezuela), within a mixed meadow of Thalassia testudinum and Halophila stipulacea located in a shallow area mangroves. Specimens were preserved in 4% formalin and identified using stereomicroscopy and taxonomic keys. A total of 29 macroalgae species (16 Rhodophyta, 11 Chlorophyta, and 2 Ochrophyta) and two filamentous cyanobacteria were recorded. Nine macroalgae species were found as epiphytes on both seagrasses, while 20 species grew on the substrate. The presence of calcareous crusts of Hydrolithon farinosum, a red alga that facilitates the establishment of other organisms, was noteworthy. Additionally, evidence of herbivory (bites and perforations) was observed on the leaves of both plants. H. stipulacea, native to the Indian Ocean, showed massive growth, occupying available substrate spaces. The grazing evidence suggests its integration into the local food web as a primary producer, similar to T. testudinum. Furthermore, the presence of epiphytes on both seagrasses demonstrates that the exotic seagrass fulfills an ecological role analogous to the native species as a substrate for other organisms.
